strengths: Addresses a practically important and well-motivated problem: adapting interactive medical image segmentation models to post-deployment distribution shift using naturally available user corrections, without requiring extra annotation effort.

The method is simple, principled, and deployable: the two-stage strategy (single-click localization followed by multi-click correction) is well aligned with the clinical interaction loop, and the computational cost is favorable (two backpropagations per image vs. ten or more for TSCA/IA+SA).

Broad and reasonably convincing empirical evaluation: 5 fundus and 4 brain MRI databases spanning modality shifts (FLAIR → T1/T1c/T2) and pathology shifts (glioma → stroke, TBI, WMH), with a baseline interactive model shared across methods for fairness.

Includes an ablation study that decomposes the contribution of each stage and the Gaussian Point Loss, including an evaluation over the adaptation sequence showing stability of the full method over time.
Reports robustness checks, e.g., performance with fewer clicks (3 iterations) and on the same-modality test set, showing adaptation does not degrade in-distribution performance.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The Gaussian Point Loss is essentially a Gaussian-weighted cross-entropy over a fixed 21×21 neighborhood around clicks, and the two-stage fine-tuning scheme is a fairly straightforward engineering combination of standard components (Dice-Focal loss, pseudo-label self-training, Adam updates). The contribution feels incremental relative to prior online/continual adaptation work (IA+SA, TSCA).

The method trains on its own final predictions (after T clicks) as pseudo ground truth, which introduces a self-training/confirmation-bias risk: systematic errors that survive the 10-click simulation could be reinforced across the adaptation sequence. The paper provides no analysis of pseudo-label quality, error accumulation, or failure cases where the base model's final prediction is substantially wrong.

Baseline coverage is narrow for the test-time adaptation literature. Only IA+SA and TSCA are compared; no comparison to generic online test-time adaptation methods (e.g., entropy minimization, TENT-style approaches) or to stronger interactive backbones (e.g., SAM-based) under the same protocol. MedSAM Adapter appears in only one table and is not an adaptation baseline.

No statistical rigor: results are averaged over only three runs, with no standard deviations or significance tests, despite some reported margins being modest (e.g., GAMMA disc at 10 clicks is essentially tied with TSCA). Sensitivity to the order of the image sequence during online adaptation is also unreported.

Key hyperparameters appear under-justified: β = 200 for the GPL weight, σ = 3, and the hard-coded ±10 pixel neighborhood are stated without analysis of sensitivity, and their appropriateness across resolutions/modalities is unclear.

Click simulation (connected-component-based point placement) may not reflect real clinician behavior, and no user study or real interaction experiment is provided; reproducibility is further limited by the private TBI dataset.

Presentation issues: the paper reads as a compressed systems description (likely page-limited), with some important details (training protocol of the base model, pseudo-label generation, multi-class handling of GPL) deferred or thin, and Fig. 1 is dense to the point of being hard to parse.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: adapting interactive segmentation models to post-deployment data distributions, which is underexplored in medical imaging.
Evaluation covers a broad set of 9 datasets (5 fundus, 4 brain MRI) spanning multiple distribution shift types (scanner, modality, pathology), which is more extensive than typical related work.
Baselines (IA+SA, TSCA, MedSAM adapter) are re-implemented on the same base interactive model with the same learning rate, making the comparison reasonably fair.
The proposed method requires fewer backpropagation steps per image than prior online adaptation methods (2 vs. 10+), which is a meaningful efficiency argument.
An ablation study dissects the contribution of the two stages and the GPL loss, including a held-out test set evaluated over the adaptation sequence.
The authors claim code and models will be released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core components are straightforward engineering: (1) a Gaussian-weighted cross-entropy in a fixed 21x21 pixel neighborhood around clicks, (2) two-round fine-tuning on pseudo-labels, and (3) standard self-training with pseudo ground truth from the model's own T-click predictions. None of these constitutes a substantive methodological advance, and the paper's framing of simplicity does not compensate for the incremental contribution.

The supervision signal is the model's own final prediction after T clicks (pseudo ground truth). This creates a well-known confirmation-bias / error-propagation risk in self-training, but the paper provides no theoretical or empirical analysis of when adaptation degrades the model (e.g., failure cases, drift on adversarial or very poor initial predictions). Only one sanity check (Flair test set, 96.3% vs. 96.4%) is given for degradation.

Key hyperparameters appear to be hard-coded and resolution-dependent: Gaussian sigma=3, the 10-pixel neighborhood cutoff, beta=200, alpha=0.7. There is no sensitivity analysis, and it is unclear how the fixed pixel window transfers across datasets with different image resolutions and object scales (fundus vs. MRI lesions), undermining the claimed reliability on 'varying new distributions without oversight by technical experts.'

All experiments use automatically simulated clicks with a deterministic click-generation heuristic (largest connected error regions). No study with real clinician/user interactions is provided, despite strong clinical-workflow claims; the gap between simulated and human click patterns is known to affect interactive segmentation conclusions.

The base model is ISFCNN, an older CNN architecture from 2019. Comparisons against modern promptable foundation models (SAM/MedSAM variants) are minimal (one MedSAM adapter row in a single table), so it is hard to assess whether online adaptation of a stronger base model would subsume the contribution.

Evaluation is restricted to 2D: only the slice with the largest lesion area per case is used, labels are merged into one class, and results are averaged Dice at click counts 1/5/10 without confidence intervals or statistical significance tests for most comparisons (only fundus results are 'averaged over three runs'). Some reported gains, e.g., TBI at 10 clicks (72.5 vs. 72.4) and GAMMA disc at 10 clicks (97.5 vs. 97.5), are within noise, yet framed as 'comparable or better.'

The two-stage design introduces a train/inference asymmetry (Stage 1 uses a single localization click as input, Stage 2 uses generated correction clicks) whose rationale is mostly empirical; the ablation shows stage 2 hurts or helps depending on click count, suggesting the design is dataset- and protocol-dependent.

Writing and presentation issues: the GPL notation is confusing (u_{i',j'} conflates a click location with an index over clicks; the mask I is defined awkwardly), Fig. 1 is dense and hard to parse, and the 'no-frills' positioning in the abstract/introduction oversells what is essentially self-training with a locality-weighted loss.

No analysis of catastrophic forgetting of the source distribution in the sequence-adaptation setting (the footnote dismisses continual learning concerns, but a deployed model that drifts on the original domain is a real deployment risk that deserves at least an experiment).

strengths: Addresses a practical and clinically relevant problem: adapting deployed interactive segmentation models to post-deployment data distributions using user corrections, which is a natural but underexplored setting in medical imaging.
The proposed method is simple and efficient: only two backpropagation steps per image versus ten (TSCA) or more (IA+SA), which is an important practical advantage for clinical workflows.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 5 fundus and 4 brain MRI databases covering multiple shift types (scanner/site shift, modality shift Flair->T1/T1c/T2, pathology shift to stroke, TBI, WMH), with consistent gains over baselines, especially under large distribution shift (e.g., +24.9% Dice over frozen model on BRATS T1 at 1 click).

Includes an ablation study that justifies both the two-stage design and the Gaussian Point Loss, including a longitudinal analysis showing the full strategy improves over the image sequence while ablated variants fluctuate or degrade.
Robustness checks with fewer clicks (3 iterations) show the method outperforms TSCA even when base predictions are poor, and no degradation is observed on in-distribution data (96.3% vs 96.4%).
Fair baseline comparison: baselines (IA+SA, TSCA) are reimplemented on the same base model with tuned learning rates, and code/models are promised for release.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the Gaussian Point Loss is a straightforward Gaussian-weighted cross-entropy around clicks, and the two-stage self-training procedure is a fairly direct combination of standard ideas (pseudo-label distillation plus click-conditioned fine-tuning); the contribution is more engineering than conceptual.

Self-training on the model's own final prediction as pseudo ground truth risks confirmation bias / error propagation; the paper does not analyze failure cases or provide any mechanism (e.g., uncertainty weighting) to mitigate this, and the dependence of adaptation quality on pseudo-label quality is not quantified.

Evaluation relies entirely on simulated clicks (largest-error-region heuristic) rather than real user studies; the simulation strategy may systematically favor the proposed adaptation scheme, and no human-in-the-loop validation is provided.
Hyperparameters of GPL (sigma=3, 10-pixel cutoff, beta=200) are fixed without ablation or sensitivity analysis, and it is unclear how sensitive performance is to these choices.

Evaluation is restricted to a single 2D slice per case (largest lesion area), which weakens clinical significance and differs from full 3D volumetric evaluation; variance is not reported despite averaging over three runs.

Only two continual-adaptation baselines (IA+SA, TSCA) plus one SAM-based adapter are compared; the MedSAM Adapter performs so poorly it functions as a weak baseline, and recent promptable-segmentation adaptation methods are not discussed or compared.

Potential instability of online learning (sensitivity to image ordering, degradation over long sequences, interplay with training-distribution forgetting) is only partially addressed by one ablation panel on G1020.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: online adaptation of interactive segmentation models to distribution shifts in medical imaging is practically relevant, and the framing (user corrections as pseudo-ground-truth) is intuitive and sensible.

Comprehensive evaluation across 9 databases (5 fundus, 4 brain-MRI) covering diverse distribution shifts (unseen scanners, modalities, and pathologies), with consistent gains over adaptation baselines (IA+SA, TSCA) and a SAM-based frozen model.

Unusually thorough ablation and robustness analysis: component-wise ablations (Tab. 5-7), hyperparameter sensitivity (Tab. 12, Fig. 6), extreme domain shift and 'worst-first' ordering (Tab. 10), noisy/wrong user clicks (Tab. 11), overfitting with 50 clicks (Tab. 8), mixed-domain adaptation (Tab. 9), source-domain stability (Tab. 17-18), clicks-to-target-Dice efficiency (Tab. 14), and computational latency.

Comparison against unsupervised pseudo-label/entropy-minimization baselines (Tab. 15-16) convincingly demonstrates that explicitly using click information is essential, addressing an obvious alternative explanation for the gains.
Fair experimental protocol: adaptation baselines use the same pretrained backbone, no per-dataset hyperparameter tuning, and code release promised, supporting reproducibility.
Practical relevance: negligible adaptation latency (even on CPU), fewer clicks to reach target Dice, and low sensitivity to hyperparameters support real-world deployment claims.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the core ideas (pseudo-label self-training, Gaussian weighting around clicks, sequential fine-tuning) are relatively simple combinations of known techniques; the CCG loss is a small design addition. The paper's value rests largely on empirical thoroughness rather than conceptual advances.

All experiments use simulated clicks; there is no user study or real clinician interaction, leaving open questions about realism (real users may stop at different quality levels, click differently, or fail to confirm quality, which the 'good enough pseudo-ground-truth' assumption depends on).

Backbone limited to a small U-Net (ICNN-style); SAM/MedSAM-based backbones are dismissed after Med-SA underperforms, but a stronger SAM-based baseline adapted with the proposed scheme is not attempted, so generality of the adaptation method across architectures remains unverified.
Baselines for online interactive adaptation are limited to IA+SA and TSCA; no comparison with broader test-time adaptation or domain adaptation methods combined with interactive segmentation.
2D-only evaluation on inherently 3D MRI data (largest-lesion slice selection) limits applicability claims to volumetric clinical workflows.

Some assumptions could interact problematically: adaptation uses the user-refined output as target, so persistent systematic user/model errors may be reinforced; the noisy-click experiments partially address this but only in simulated form.
Some gains on fundus data are modest (near-saturated disc Dice), with the main improvements concentrated on MRI settings.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: adapting interactive segmentation models to distribution shifts encountered at deployment in medical imaging, which is underexplored relative to automatic segmentation adaptation.

Evaluation scope is broad: 5 fundus and 4 brain-MRI databases spanning modality shifts (FLAIR vs. T1/T1c/T2) and pathology shifts (glioma, stroke, WMH, TBI), covering both small and large distribution gaps.

Baselines are handled fairly: TSCA and IA+SA are re-implemented on the same CCG-pretrained backbone as the proposed method, isolating the contribution of the adaptation strategy itself; Med-SA is included as a SAM-based comparison.

The core empirical result is convincing in the large-shift regime: on BRATS T1, PI+MI reaches 71.2/83.4/88.0 Dice at 1/5/10 clicks versus 34.4/60.9/74.0 for TSCA, and the method reaches an 80% Dice target with roughly half the clicks of TSCA (Table 14).

Ablations are thorough: each loss term and adaptation stage is ablated (Table 5), the CCG design choices (Gaussian kernel, class-limited masking, sigma) are analyzed (Tables 6-7, Fig. 6), and hyperparameter sensitivity is reported (Table 12).

Robustness analyses go beyond the standard setup: extreme domain shift with near-zero initial Dice, worst-first image ordering, wrong-class clicks, overfitting under 50 clicks, mixed-database adaptation, and source-domain non-degradation (Tables 8-11, 17-18), plus a comparison against unsupervised pseudo-label/entropy-minimization losses in the appendix.
Practicality is considered: computational latency is measured on both GPU and CPU and remains negligible relative to interactive workflows.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The method is a combination of well-known ideas: pseudo-labeling from user-refined predictions (Kontogianni et al. 2020 already adapt from corrections), Gaussian-smoothed click encoding (ICNN), and Dice-Focal loss. The CCG loss is a straightforward Gaussian-weighted cross-entropy restricted to same-class pixels. The main delta over TSCA/IA+SA is optimizing against the full refined mask rather than sparse clicked pixels, which is an incremental design change rather than a new insight.

All experiments rely on oracle-based click simulation: clicks are placed at the center of the largest erroneous connected component computed against the ground truth (Appendix A.2). This simulator is significantly more informative and consistent than real clinicians, who click noisily and may not target the largest error first. Given that the entire framework hinges on the quality of user-refined outputs as pseudo-ground-truth, the absence of any human study or even a degraded/noisy-click simulation in the main experiments substantially weakens the central claim of practical effectiveness.

Gains in the small-shift fundus regime are modest and sometimes mixed: on GS1 and GAMMA the method is roughly on par with TSCA (e.g., GAMMA at 1 click, PI+MI 95.1/85.8 vs. TSCA 94.6/84.2), and PI+MI is occasionally slightly worse than PI (e.g., GS1 Cup at 1 and 10 clicks). The strong claims mostly rest on the brain-MRI results, where the shift is severe; the paper would benefit from a clearer characterization of when the approach does and does not help.

The evaluation uses only Dice on a single 2D slice per 3D case (the slice with the largest lesion area), which inflates apparent performance relative to volumetric segmentation practice and omits boundary-sensitive metrics (e.g., HD95) that matter for clinical use.

The key assumption that P_final is 'good enough' as pseudo-ground-truth is asserted rather than validated: the paper does not quantify pseudo-label error rates, nor does it provide a mechanism (e.g., a quality gate or uncertainty check) to reject poor refinements, leaving potential error accumulation under-addressed beyond the worst-ordering sanity check.

Mid-Interaction adaptation updates all model parameters after every click during an ongoing interaction; while latencies are small, the paper does not analyze whether sequential in-interaction weight updates could destabilize predictions within a single image in edge cases, nor compare against lighter alternatives (e.g., updating only decoder or BN parameters).

Hyperparameters (alpha=0.7, beta=200, sigma=3) were chosen in 'preliminary experiments,' and Table 12 shows noticeable sensitivity on BRATS T1 (e.g., beta=100 drops Dice to 81.3 vs. 87.4 at beta=400); the claim of no per-database tuning is welcome but the selection procedure is not fully specified.

Positioning against the interactive segmentation and test-time adaptation literature is somewhat narrow; connections to test-time adaptation techniques (e.g., entropy minimization is tested only as a baseline, other TTA regularizers are not considered) and to scribble/box-prompt interactive methods are not explored despite being mentioned as future work.

strengths: Well-motivated and practical problem: online adaptation of interactive segmentation under distribution shift is clinically relevant, and the observation that user-corrected outputs can serve as pseudo-ground-truth is a clean, useful insight.

Comprehensive evaluation across 9 databases spanning two imaging types (fundus and brain MRI) with diverse shift types (across scanners, modalities, and pathologies), including very challenging extreme-shift settings (e.g., Flair->ATLAS-T1 starting at 9.3% Dice).

Consistent and often large improvements over the strongest available baselines (IA+SA, TSCA), with gains exceeding 10% Dice on brain MRI, plus a click-efficiency analysis (clicks needed to reach target Dice).

Thorough ablation studies covering every loss term and stage (Table 5), design choices of the CCG loss (Table 7, sigma ablation), and hyperparameter sensitivity (Table 12), supporting the soundness of the design.

Unusually strong robustness analyses: overfitting with 50 clicks, worst-case image ordering, noisy/wrong user clicks, performance on source-domain data, and re-adaptation back to the source — these address the main risks of pseudo-label-based online learning.

Practicality is demonstrated via computational latency measurements (negligible overhead even on CPU), and the method is model-agnostic with clear algorithmic descriptions enabling reproduction; code release is promised.
weaknesses: Moderate conceptual novelty: the core ideas (pseudo-label self-training on user-corrected predictions, Gaussian-weighted loss around clicks, online adaptation after each image) are relatively straightforward combinations of known techniques; the contribution is more engineering/systematic than conceptually new.

The backbone is a simple U-Net ICNN-style (2019) architecture; no experiments demonstrating that OAIMS transfers to modern promptable architectures (SAM/MedSAM variants), which limits claims of generality and leaves the practical relevance to current interactive tools uncertain.
Only user simulations are used; no study with real human annotators/clinicians, so the key assumption that P_final is 'good enough' as pseudo-ground-truth is validated only in simulation.

Main results tables (Tables 1-4) appear to report single-run averages without standard deviations or confidence intervals (only Table 6 uses 3 seeds), which weakens the statistical strength of the reported gains, some of which are small (e.g., fundus GS1/GAMMA).

Baseline set is somewhat narrow: comparisons are limited to IA+SA and TSCA (plus a frozen Med-SA that underperforms); no comparison with other test-time adaptation or test-time training approaches applied to this setting.
Evaluation uses only the 2D slice with largest lesion area per case rather than full 3D volumes, which reduces clinical realism for MRI.

Some methodological details warrant more justification, e.g., the choice of beta=200 (a large loss weight), the single-source-database setup, and the fixed number of stages in Post-Interaction adaptation; sensitivity is shown but rationale could be stronger.
